title: Scientists Unveil Foot‑Stiffening Socks That Reduce Walking Fatigue, Boost Endurance【ScienceAlert】
body:
A team of biomechanical engineers has unveiled a novel “smart” sock that gently compresses the ball of the foot, stiffening the arch and cutting the energy cost of each step. Laboratory tests show the garment can shave up to 5 percent of the metabolic expenditure required for walking, a gain that could translate into longer, less tiring strides for athletes, older adults, and anyone who spends a lot of time on their feet.

The prototype, developed at the University of Queensland’s Centre for Human Motion Research, integrates a thin, elastic band woven into the fabric of a standard cotton sock. When the wearer lifts their heel, the band tightens around the metatarsal heads, momentarily raising the longitudinal arch. This biomechanical tweak mirrors the natural “wind‑up” that elite runners use to store elastic energy in the foot’s spring‑like structures. By artificially augmenting that spring, the sock reduces the amount of muscular work the calf and foot muscles must perform, allowing the body to recycle more of the kinetic energy generated with each step.

To quantify the effect, researchers recruited 20 healthy volunteers and equipped them with indirect calorimetry masks while they walked on a treadmill at a comfortable pace, both with and without the arch‑supporting socks. The data revealed a consistent drop in oxygen consumption—averaging 0.3 millilitres per kilogram per minute—when participants wore the compression garment. In practical terms, a person weighing 70 kilograms could save roughly 10 kilojoules of energy over a ten‑kilometre walk, equivalent to the caloric cost of a small snack. The benefit was most pronounced in participants with naturally lower arch stiffness, suggesting the technology could be especially advantageous for individuals whose foot mechanics are less efficient.

The concept builds on decades of research into foot biomechanics, where the arch has long been recognized as a critical energy‑return structure. Traditional orthotics and supportive shoes attempt to enhance this function by rigidly holding the arch in place, often at the expense of comfort or natural foot motion. The new sock takes a subtler approach, applying just enough pressure to assist the arch without immobilizing it. This dynamic assistance preserves the foot’s ability to adapt to uneven terrain, a limitation that has hampered previous attempts to “mechanically boost” walking efficiency.

Beyond everyday use, the technology could have far‑reaching implications for specific populations. Elderly individuals, who often experience reduced muscular strength and altered gait patterns, might benefit from the reduced metabolic load, potentially lowering fall risk by decreasing fatigue. Military personnel and disaster‑response workers, who must march long distances carrying heavy loads, could see measurable improvements in endurance. Even competitive runners are eyeing the sock as a low‑profile performance aid that sidesteps the regulatory bans placed on more overt exoskeletons and powered footwear.

The research team is now moving from the lab to real‑world testing, partnering with a sports apparel company to refine the design for mass production. Future iterations aim to incorporate smart textiles that adjust compression in response to gait phase detection, delivering personalized assistance without manual intervention. If these developments prove successful, the humble sock could become a quiet yet powerful tool in the quest to make human locomotion more efficient, ushering in a new era where everyday footwear subtly amplifies the body’s own biomechanics.
